questions.question:
D1 — Complexity gate: 5 new classes for a behavior-preserving refactor, or fewer?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor plan (PLAN.md), reorganizing tenant-auth orchestration with no product behavior change.
ELI10: The plan says its goal is to move existing auth code around without changing what users experience, but it introduces five new classes across twelve files. Two of those classes look like they do not earn a class: RequestPolicy is described by the plan itself as stateless with no side effects (that is a function), and TokenStore is never described while AuthCache already wraps the one backing cache. Every extra class is another seam a tired engineer has to trace at 3am when a tenant cannot log in.
Stakes if we pick wrong: too many classes and the refactor ships with duplicated cache-like surfaces (TokenStore vs AuthCache) and a class-shaped wrapper around one pure decision; too few and a genuinely distinct responsibility (if TokenStore has one) gets crammed into AuthCache and re-split later.
Recommendation: A because the plan's own description of RequestPolicy (PLAN.md:12-13) is the definition of a pure function, and TokenStore has no stated responsibility distinct from AuthCache (PLAN.md:20-21, 45).
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
This chooses structure only. Contracts stay fixed (PLAN.md:16-22); the shared mutable AuthCache, the nested try/catch, the regression coverage and the Promise.all change are separate remedies asked later, not decided here.
Pros / cons:
A) 3 units: AuthBroker, SessionMint, AuthCache; RequestPolicy becomes a pure function; TokenStore folded into AuthCache (recommended)
  ✅ One cache-facing surface instead of two, so invalidation on logout/revocation/suspension has one place to be right
  ✅ Access decision is a pure `decideAccess(claims, ctx)` function: trivially unit-testable, no lifecycle, no mocks
  ❌ If TokenStore turns out to own something the adapter does not (e.g. refresh-token persistence), you rediscover it mid-implementation and re-split
B) 4 units: AuthBroker, SessionMint, AuthCache, TokenStore; RequestPolicy becomes a pure function
  ✅ Keeps TokenStore's seam available in case it holds a responsibility the plan did not write down
  ✅ Still removes the class wrapper around a stateless decision, the clearest over-abstraction in the plan
  ❌ Two token-holding abstractions remain in one refactor with no written contract distinguishing them; DRY risk is real
C) Original arrangement: all 5 classes as written (AuthBroker, TokenStore, SessionMint, AuthCache, RequestPolicy)
  ✅ Matches the author's mental model exactly; no re-planning cost before implementation starts
  ✅ RequestPolicy as a class leaves room to grow if policy is expected to gain state or dependencies later
  ❌ Five new seams for a refactor whose stated goal is no behavior change; two of them are unjustified by the plan text
Net: trading a small chance of re-splitting TokenStore against carrying two undescribed or unnecessary abstractions into a security-sensitive codepath.

options.label: A) 3 units (recommended)
options.description: AuthBroker, SessionMint, AuthCache as classes. RequestPolicy becomes a pure exported function decideAccess(claims, ctx) in a policy module. TokenStore folds into AuthCache (one facade over the one backing adapter). Structure only; all other remedies stay pending.

options.label: B) 4 units
options.description: AuthBroker, SessionMint, AuthCache, TokenStore as classes. RequestPolicy becomes a pure exported function. TokenStore kept as its own seam; the plan must then state its responsibility distinct from AuthCache. Structure only; all other remedies stay pending.

options.label: C) Original 5 classes
options.description: Keep AuthBroker, TokenStore, SessionMint, AuthCache, RequestPolicy exactly as the plan lists them across 12 files. Structure only; all other remedies stay pending.

questions.question:
D2 — How should AuthBroker and SessionMint get the shared AuthCache: injected, or a module-level global?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor plan (PLAN.md); D1 fixed the structure at 3 units (AuthBroker, SessionMint, AuthCache + decideAccess function).
ELI10: Right now the plan has one cache object living at the top of a module, and both services reach out and grab it. That works until you want to test one service alone, run two tenants' worth of fixtures in one test file, or swap the cache backend: every test shares the same hidden object and leaks state into the next one. Handing the cache in through the constructor makes the dependency visible and gives you one obvious place (the composition root) where the single instance is created.
Stakes if we pick wrong: with the global, a flaky test suite and a cache that cannot be replaced without editing the module; with injection done sloppily, two call sites accidentally construct two AuthCache instances over one adapter and invalidation only hits one.
Recommendation: A because a security-sensitive cache should have exactly one construction site and every consumer should declare it; this is the explicit-over-clever preference with almost no extra effort (human: ~2h / CC: ~10 min).
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
This decides wiring only. The write-after-invalidate guard (R2) is asked next; structure stays at D1's 3 units.
Pros / cons:
A) Constructor injection from one composition root (recommended)
  ✅ Each service declares its cache dependency; unit tests construct a fresh AuthCache over a fake adapter per test
  ✅ Exactly one `new AuthCache(adapter)` call site, so the "one backing cache" contract (PLAN.md:21) is enforced by construction
  ❌ Every place that instantiates AuthBroker or SessionMint must pass the cache; a handful of call sites change
B) Module-level export as planned
  ✅ Zero wiring changes; matches the plan text exactly and is the fastest path to a green build
  ✅ Guarantees a single instance by module semantics without a composition root
  ❌ Hidden coupling and cross-test state leakage; replacing the adapter means editing the module, not the wiring
C) Module-level export plus an explicit `resetForTests()` hook
  ✅ Keeps the plan's import-and-use ergonomics while giving tests a way to clear shared state
  ✅ Smallest change that addresses the test-isolation symptom
  ❌ Test-only hooks in production auth code are a smell; the dependency is still invisible at the call site
Net: trading a few constructor-signature edits against a hidden global in the codepath that decides who gets into which tenant.

options.label: A) Constructor injection (recommended)
options.description: One composition root creates a single `AuthCache(adapter)` and passes it to `new AuthBroker(cache, ...)` and `new SessionMint(cache, ...)`. No module-level export of the instance. Tests construct their own AuthCache over a fake adapter. Wiring only; R2 guard stays pending.

options.label: B) Module-level export
options.description: Keep the plan as written: `AuthCache` instance exported from its module and imported by both services. Wiring only; R2 guard stays pending.

options.label: C) Module global + resetForTests()
options.description: Keep the module-level export and add an explicit `resetForTests()` that swaps or clears the shared instance for test isolation. Wiring only; R2 guard stays pending.

questions.question:
D3 — Should AuthCache refuse a cache write that started before an invalidation for the same tenant?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor plan (PLAN.md); D1 fixed 3 units, D2 fixed constructor injection of one AuthCache.
ELI10: Two services write into the same cache and the plan says nothing serializes those writes. Picture tenant T getting suspended: the invalidation hook wipes T's entries, but SessionMint was already halfway through minting a session for T and writes a fresh entry a few milliseconds later. That entry survives until it expires, so a suspended tenant keeps getting in. The fix is a small stamp: each tenant has an invalidation counter, a write remembers the counter it saw when it started, and the cache drops the write if the counter moved.
Stakes if we pick wrong: without the guard, logout, revocation and suspension can be silently undone by a racing write and nobody sees an error; with the guard done wrong, legitimate writes get dropped and users see extra IDP round trips (a cache miss, not a lockout).
Recommendation: A because the failure is silent, security-relevant, and the guard is a few lines inside the one facade that D1 and D2 just made the single write path (human: ~1 day incl. tests / CC: ~20 min).
Completeness: A=10/10, B=3/10, C=n/a (investigation only, no remedy)
Pros / cons:
A) Per-tenant invalidation generation with compare-and-set writes in AuthCache (recommended)
  ✅ Suspension, revocation and logout cannot be resurrected by a racing mint or validation write; the invariant lives in one place
  ✅ Failure mode degrades to a cache miss (one extra IDP call), never to a wrongly cached allow
  ❌ Adds state to the facade (a generation map) and a deterministic concurrency test that must be written carefully
B) No guard; both services write directly as planned
  ✅ Smallest diff; keeps the facade a thin pass-through over the adapter exactly as PLAN.md:20-21 describes
  ✅ If the legacy flow already had this race, this option does not make anything worse than today
  ❌ A suspended or logged-out tenant can retain cached access until expiry with no log line; silent security regression risk
C) Investigate first: bounded probe of the existing adapter's ordering guarantees, then decide
  ✅ Avoids building a guard the adapter may already provide (e.g. versioned keys or invalidate-then-fence semantics)
  ✅ Cheap: read the adapter and its invalidation tests, report what ordering exists (CC: ~5 min once source is available)
  ❌ Leaves the race unresolved in the plan until the probe runs; implementation must not start this seam before the follow-up answer
Net: trading a small generation map and one concurrency test against a silent way for revoked access to come back.

options.label: A) Generation guard (recommended)
options.description: AuthCache keeps a per-tenant invalidation generation; every invalidation hook (logout, revocation, suspension) bumps it; `put()` carries the generation observed at read time and is dropped if the tenant's generation has advanced. Includes the deterministic concurrency test. Applies inside the facade only.

options.label: B) No guard
options.description: Both services write to AuthCache directly with no ordering check, as the plan describes. Race is recorded as an accepted risk in the report.

options.label: C) Investigate first
options.description: Bounded probe of the existing adapter and its invalidation tests for ordering guarantees before choosing. Approves no implementation; the guard choice stays pending for a follow-up answer.

questions.question:
D4 — How should validateAndDispatch() handle errors: one explicit error map, or keep the nested try/catch?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor plan (PLAN.md); structure, wiring and the cache guard are fixed (D1–D3).
ELI10: The function that decides whether a request gets in has three try/catch blocks nested inside each other, and each one quietly eats a different kind of error. When an error is eaten, the code after it keeps running as if nothing went wrong, so a failed token check can fall through to dispatch, or fail with no log line to explain a locked-out user. The fix is to make the flow a straight line (validate, decide, dispatch) and have one place that says, for each error type, exactly what the caller gets back and what gets logged.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a swallowed validation error can become an allow (security), and a swallowed IDP outage becomes a silent lockout with no log to debug at 3am.
Recommendation: A because deny-by-default with an explicit error map is the smallest change that makes every failure path both safe and visible; it also drops the function well under 60 lines (human: ~4h / CC: ~15 min).
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=2/10
Pros / cons:
A) Linear flow with one explicit error map, deny-by-default, structured logs (recommended)
  ✅ Every error class has a named outcome (e.g. ValidationError → deny 401, PolicyDenied → deny 403, IdpUnavailable → 503 + retryable) and a log line with tenant and request IDs
  ✅ Unknown errors deny and re-throw, so nothing new can slip through to dispatch; table-driven tests cover each row
  ❌ Callers that relied on a swallowed error producing a soft result may see a new explicit deny; the regression suite must catch this
B) Keep the nested blocks; each catch logs and returns an explicit deny
  ✅ Minimal structural change to a function the team already knows
  ✅ Stops the silent-swallow behavior, which is the most dangerous part
  ❌ Still 60 lines and three nesting levels; the outcome for each error class is spread across the function instead of one table
C) Keep as described: nested blocks that swallow
  ✅ Zero risk of changing any caller-visible behavior in this refactor
  ✅ No new tests required for this function beyond what the plan already lists
  ❌ Errors keep disappearing in the codepath that grants access; incompatible with the "explicit over clever" preference
Net: trading a small chance that a caller depended on a swallowed error against silent failures in the access-granting path.

options.label: A) Explicit error map (recommended)
options.description: Rewrite validateAndDispatch() as validate → decideAccess → dispatch inside one try; a single catch maps each known error class to an explicit outcome and structured log; unknown errors deny and re-throw. Table-driven unit test per error class.

options.label: B) Log-and-deny in each catch
options.description: Keep the three nested try/catch blocks; replace each swallow with a log line and an explicit deny result. No restructuring.

options.label: C) Keep as described
options.description: Leave validateAndDispatch() as the plan describes it; swallowing behavior recorded as an accepted risk.

questions.question:
D5 — Should the read → miss → load → write sequence live once in AuthCache.getOrLoad(), or in each service?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor plan (PLAN.md); D1–D4 fixed structure, injection, the generation guard and the error map.
ELI10: Both AuthBroker and SessionMint need the same dance: look in the cache, if it is not there ask the IDP, then store the answer. If each service writes that dance itself, the generation guard from D3 has to be remembered in two places and a future fix lands in one and not the other. Putting the dance in one method on the cache facade means the guard is applied automatically wherever a load happens.
Stakes if we pick wrong: with duplication, one service eventually bypasses the guard or diverges on key construction and a tenant-key bug appears in only one flow; with a bad abstraction, a loader signature too generic for the two real callers.
Recommendation: A because the two callers are known now, the guard from D3 must wrap every write, and one helper is the DRY-aggressive default for this codebase (human: ~3h / CC: ~10 min).
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10, C=n/a (deferral, no remedy)
Pros / cons:
A) One `AuthCache.getOrLoad(key, loader)` used by both services (recommended)
  ✅ The D3 generation guard and the tenant/issuer/audience/policy-version key construction are applied in exactly one place
  ✅ Both services shrink to "call getOrLoad with my loader"; tests for the miss path are written once
  ❌ A loader callback is one more indirection to read; if the two callers turn out to need different miss semantics the helper grows a flag
B) Each service keeps its own read/miss/write sequence
  ✅ Each flow stays fully explicit at its own call site with no callback indirection
  ✅ No shared helper to design before the two callers exist
  ❌ Two copies of the miss path; the guard and key rules must be maintained twice and tested twice
C) Defer until duplication is confirmed in code
  ✅ Avoids abstracting on an inference; the plan text does not literally show both sequences
  ✅ Cheap to revisit once the first service is written
  ❌ Leaves the guard-application rule unowned during implementation; the second service may ship before the revisit
Net: trading a small callback indirection against maintaining the security-relevant miss path in two places.

options.label: A) getOrLoad in AuthCache (recommended)
options.description: Add `AuthCache.getOrLoad(key, loader)`: read; on miss call loader; write through the R2 generation guard. AuthBroker and SessionMint both use it for their cache-miss sequences. Tested once in AuthCache.

options.label: B) Per-service sequences
options.description: Each service implements its own read → miss → IDP → write against AuthCache.get/put. Guard and key rules maintained at both sites.

options.label: C) Defer
options.description: Implement per-service first; revisit consolidation when the duplication is confirmed in code. Approves no consolidation now.

questions.question:
D6 — How do we prove the rewritten auth flow behaves exactly like legacyAuthFlow() before the old one is deleted?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor plan (PLAN.md); D1–D5 fixed structure, injection, guard, error map and getOrLoad.
ELI10: The plan rewrites the function every tenant login goes through and, as written, has no test that says "the new one answers the same as the old one." The way to get that safely is to write the tests against the OLD function first, so they capture what it actually does today (including its quirks), then point the same tests at the new function. For an auth path you can go one step further and run both in production for a while, letting the old one decide while logging any disagreement.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a tenant that could log in yesterday cannot today, or a token that should be rejected is accepted, and there is no test that would have caught it before deploy.
Recommendation: B because characterization tests catch what you thought of and the shadow compare catches what you did not; on an auth path the extra flag is cheap insurance and is removed when the window closes (A: human ~1.5 days / CC ~30 min; B: human ~3 days / CC ~45 min).
Completeness: A=9/10, B=10/10, C=5/10
Pros / cons:
A) Characterization suite captured from legacyAuthFlow() first, then run against the new flow
  ✅ Locks in every listed outcome class before a line of the rewrite exists; failures point at the exact diverging case
  ✅ Also serves as the acceptance suite for D4: every intentionally changed outcome is listed and asserted as changed, nothing changes silently
  ❌ Only covers cases someone thought to write; real token shapes and IDP behaviors in production may differ
B) A plus a flag-gated shadow compare in production for a bounded window (recommended)
  ✅ Real traffic across real tenants checks the rewrite against the legacy decision; mismatches are logged with tenant and case, never enforced
  ✅ Reversible by construction: legacy stays authoritative until the flag flips, so rollback is a config change
  ❌ Adds a flag, a compare hook and a cleanup task; doubles IDP calls during the window unless the compare reuses the cached result
C) Happy-path characterization only (valid and expired token)
  ✅ Fast to write and covers the two most common outcomes users hit every day
  ✅ Still better than the plan's zero regression coverage
  ❌ Revocation, suspension, cross-tenant and IDP-failure paths, the ones with security consequences, remain unproven
Net: trading a temporary flag and compare hook against discovering an auth regression from a tenant's support ticket.

options.label: A) Characterization suite
options.description: Write the regression suite against legacyAuthFlow() before the rewrite covering valid, expired, revoked, logged-out, suspended tenant, cross-tenant, policy-version bump, malformed token, IDP unavailable and IDP timeout; assert outcome class and cache state. The new flow must pass it; intentional D4 differences are listed and asserted explicitly.

options.label: B) Characterization + shadow compare (recommended)
options.description: Everything in A, plus a flag-gated shadow mode where the new flow runs alongside legacy in production for a bounded window; legacy decides, mismatches are logged and alerted; the flag flips only after a clean window; flag and legacy are removed afterwards.

options.label: C) Happy path only
options.description: Characterization tests for valid and expired token only. The remaining legacy outcomes are recorded as unproven in the report.

questions.question:
D7 — How deep should the integration test for the new flow go: a two-tenant end-to-end scenario, or component-level only?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor plan (PLAN.md); D1–D6 fixed structure, wiring, guard, error map, getOrLoad and the regression suite.
ELI10: Unit tests prove each piece works alone; the bugs in auth systems usually live in the seams, like tenant A's suspension accidentally clearing tenant B's sessions, or the cache key missing one field so two tenants share an entry. One end-to-end test that runs two tenants through the whole login-to-dispatch path with a fake identity provider catches exactly those seam bugs. It is the kind of test you want to fail in CI, not in a customer's browser.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a cross-tenant leak or a suspension that does not stick reaches production because every unit test passed in isolation.
Recommendation: A because auth flows spanning 3+ components are the textbook E2E case and the fake IDP makes it deterministic (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min).
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10
Pros / cons:
A) Two-tenant E2E against a fake IDP, including suspension mid-session, cross-tenant token, IDP outage and policy-version bump (recommended)
  ✅ Exercises AuthBroker, decideAccess, AuthCache (with the D3 guard), SessionMint and dispatch together across two tenants
  ✅ Failure modes that matter to real users (suspension not sticking, cross-tenant leak, IDP down) are asserted end to end
  ❌ Needs a fake IDP fixture and takes longer per run than unit tests; must stay deterministic (no real network)
B) Component-level integration only
  ✅ Each unit is verified against fake collaborators quickly; no fixture for a full IDP conversation
  ✅ Matches the plan's wording of "unit and integration coverage" with minimal extra scope
  ❌ Seam bugs between units (key construction, invalidation propagation, dispatch after deny) are not exercised together
Net: trading one fake-IDP fixture against finding tenant-isolation bugs only in production.

options.label: A) Two-tenant E2E (recommended)
options.description: One end-to-end test file against a fake IDP: tenants A and B log in, validate, decideAccess and dispatch; cross-tenant token rejected; suspending A mid-session denies A's next request and leaves B untouched; IDP outage yields the explicit 503 path; policy-version bump forces a re-validate. Plus the common-work facade contract tests.

options.label: B) Component-level only
options.description: Integration tests per unit against fake adapter and fake IDP; no cross-unit scenario. Plus the common-work facade contract tests.

questions.question:
D8 — When should the 5 IDP calls be parallelized: as a separate final commit after regression is green, deferred, or inline in the refactor?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor plan (PLAN.md); D1–D7 fixed structure, wiring, guard, error map, getOrLoad, regression suite and E2E depth.
ELI10: Making five calls at once instead of one after another is a real speed win for every login, but it is also a behavior change: errors arrive in a different order, five requests hit the identity provider at the same instant, and if one call secretly needs another's answer it breaks. The plan's goal is "no behavior change," so the clean move is to finish the reorganization, prove it matches the old flow with the regression suite, then flip to parallel in its own commit where any difference is obviously caused by that one change.
Stakes if we pick wrong: mixed into the refactor, a regression-suite failure could be either the restructure or the parallelization and you cannot tell which; deferred forever, users keep paying five round trips on every validation.
Recommendation: A because it keeps structural and behavioral changes in separate commits (Beck) while still landing the win on this branch; the probe of independence and IDP limits is a few minutes once source is available (human: ~half day / CC: ~15 min).
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Separate final commit after the regression suite is green, gated on the independence and rate-limit probe (recommended)
  ✅ A regression failure after this commit has exactly one cause; rollback is one revert with the refactor intact
  ✅ The "calls are independent" claim is checked against source, and IDP concurrency limits are confirmed before five simultaneous requests ship
  ❌ One extra commit and a short probe before the latency win lands
B) Keep sequential in this refactor; defer parallelization to a TODO
  ✅ The branch stays a pure reorganization with zero timing or error-ordering change
  ✅ No IDP rate-limit risk introduced by this work
  ❌ A known 5x-round-trip latency cost on every validation stays in production with no scheduled fix
C) Promise.all inline in the refactor commit as the plan proposes
  ✅ Fewest commits; the win ships with the refactor
  ✅ No separate PR or coordination step
  ❌ Mixes a behavior change into a "no behavior change" refactor; regression-suite failures become ambiguous and the independence claim ships unverified
Net: trading one extra commit and a short probe against ambiguous regression failures in the auth path.

options.label: A) Separate final commit (recommended)
options.description: Land Promise.all as its own last commit on this branch after the D6 characterization suite is green against the new flow. Preconditions: bounded probe confirms no call consumes another's output and the IDP tolerates 5 concurrent calls per validation; fail-fast semantics, first rejection routed through the D4 error map; before/after latency recorded in the PR.

options.label: B) Defer to TODO
options.description: Keep the 5 calls sequential in this refactor. Parallelization becomes a TODO with the same preconditions. No timing change on this branch.

options.label: C) Inline in refactor
options.description: Apply Promise.all inside the refactor commit as the plan proposes; no independence probe required beforehand.

questions.question:
D9 — TODO: capture "flag-gated shadow compare of the new auth flow against legacyAuthFlow() in production" for later?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor plan (PLAN.md); D6 approved the characterization suite without the production shadow compare.
ELI10: You chose to prove the rewrite with tests written against the old code. The other half of the idea, running both old and new in production for a while and logging any disagreement, was not taken. This question is only about whether to write that idea down properly so a future session can pick it up with the reasoning intact, not about doing it now.
Stakes if we pick wrong: skip it and the idea evaporates; capture it badly and someone later wonders why it exists.
Recommendation: A because it costs one paragraph now and is the standard next step if the characterization suite ever misses a production-only token shape.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
What: flag-gated shadow mode where the new flow runs alongside legacyAuthFlow() for a bounded window; legacy decides; mismatches logged with tenant and case; flag flips after a clean window, then flag and legacy are deleted.
Why: catches production-only token shapes and IDP behaviors the characterization suite did not anticipate; makes cutover reversible by config.
Pros: real-traffic proof across all tenants; rollback is a config change.
Cons: temporary flag and compare hook; doubles IDP calls during the window unless the compare reuses the cached result; cleanup task.
Context: D6 in this review approved characterization tests (10 scenarios) as the regression contract. If the suite passes but any post-cutover incident shows a divergence, this is the next tool. Start at the composition root (D2) where both flows can be constructed side by side.
Depends on / blocked by: the characterization suite (D6) green against the new flow; legacyAuthFlow() must still exist when shadow mode is added.
Pros / cons:
A) Add to TODOS.md (recommended)
  ✅ Idea and its reasoning survive with a clear starting point (composition root) and trigger
  ✅ Zero implementation cost now; does not change any approved scope
  ❌ TODOS.md cannot be written in plan mode; content is presented as not persisted until you leave plan mode
B) Skip — not valuable enough
  ✅ Keeps the TODO list focused if you are confident the suite is sufficient
  ✅ Nothing to maintain or clean up later
  ❌ The reasoning is lost; a future incident re-derives it from scratch
C) Build it now in this branch
  ✅ Maximum rollout safety for an auth cutover
  ✅ The flag and compare hook are small once the composition root exists
  ❌ Reopens D6's accepted scope and adds a flag and cleanup task to a branch whose goal is a reorganization
Net: one paragraph of captured reasoning versus nothing.

options.label: A) Add to TODOS.md (recommended)
options.description: Record the What/Why/Pros/Cons/Context/Depends block above in TODOS.md (presented as not persisted while in plan mode). No implementation now.

options.label: B) Skip
options.description: Do not capture; the idea is dropped from this review's outputs.

options.label: C) Build it now
options.description: Reopen D6 and add the flag-gated shadow compare to this branch's accepted scope; a follow-up decision will re-record R5.

questions.question:
D10 — TODO: capture "single-flight de-duplication of concurrent cache misses in AuthCache.getOrLoad()" for later?
Project/branch/task: main — Multi-tenant Auth Refactor plan (PLAN.md); D5 approved getOrLoad as the single miss path.
ELI10: When a tenant's policy version changes, every cached token for that tenant becomes a miss at the same moment, and every in-flight request asks the identity provider separately. Single-flight means the first miss for a key does the IDP call and the others wait for that same answer. It is an existing cost, not something this refactor introduces, but D5 just created the one place where it would be a small change. This question is only about writing it down.
Stakes if we pick wrong: skip and a busy tenant's policy bump keeps producing an IDP burst nobody remembers is avoidable; capture and the fix has an obvious home.
Recommendation: A because getOrLoad is the right home and the reasoning is cheap to keep; building now would add behavior to a reorganization branch.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
What: per-key in-flight promise map inside AuthCache.getOrLoad(); concurrent misses for the same key share one loader call; entry cleared on settle.
Why: a policy-version bump or cold start for a large tenant turns N concurrent requests into N IDP calls; single-flight makes it 1.
Pros: cuts IDP load and tail latency during invalidation storms; lives in the one approved miss path.
Cons: in-process only (no cross-instance de-dup); must respect the D3 generation guard (a shared result observed before an invalidation must still be dropped); needs a concurrency test.
Context: D5 approved `AuthCache.getOrLoad(key, loader)` as the single read → miss → load → write path. Add the in-flight map there; the generation check on write already exists (D3). Measure IDP call count during a policy bump before and after.
Depends on / blocked by: getOrLoad landed (D5); the D8 parallelization commit (to avoid two performance changes in one measurement).
Pros / cons:
A) Add to TODOS.md (recommended)
  ✅ Fix has a named home (getOrLoad) and a named trigger (policy-version bump burst) for whoever picks it up
  ✅ No change to any approved scope on this branch
  ❌ Not persisted while in plan mode; the IDP burst remains until someone picks it up
B) Skip — not valuable enough
  ✅ Keeps the TODO list focused if policy bumps are rare and tenants are small
  ✅ Nothing to maintain
  ❌ Existing IDP burst cost stays unrecorded
C) Build it now in this branch

# Plan: Multi-tenant Auth Refactor — Reviewed Implementation Plan

Reviewed target: `PLAN.md` ("Plan: Multi-tenant Auth Refactor") in `/tmp/g-6jt867_i/gstack-paid-shard-Lij831/tmp/gstack-plan-count-WtrIYR`, branch `main`, commit `5c885d6`.
Review: `/plan-eng-review`, 2026-09-16. Evidence base: the plan text only — the repository contains no source or tests, so every finding cites `PLAN.md:line` and marks runtime behavior unknown where the plan does not state it.

## Context
The goal is to reorganize existing tenant-auth orchestration without changing
its product behavior (`PLAN.md:8-9`). The per-request access decision takes
already-fetched claims plus tenant/request context and returns allow or deny
under the existing access policy; `AuthBroker.validateAndDispatch()` calls it
after validation and before dispatch. It adds no policy, network call, cache
mutation or state (`PLAN.md:9-13`).

## Existing contracts retained (unchanged)
The existing cache adapter keys entries by tenant ID, issuer, audience, and
policy version. It evicts expired tokens and invalidates entries on logout,
token revocation, or tenant suspension. `AuthCache` retains these validity and
tenant-key rules unchanged; the adapter does not serialize mutations.
`AuthCache` is a service-facing facade over that same existing adapter, with
one backing cache. The adapter, its invalidation hooks, and their existing
tests remain in use unchanged (`PLAN.md:16-22`).

## Architecture (amended by D1)
Structure chosen at D1 (scope reduced): **3 units**, not 5 classes.

| Unit | Kind | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| `AuthBroker` | class | `validateAndDispatch()`: validate token, call `decideAccess`, dispatch |
| `SessionMint` | class | mint/refresh sessions; reads and writes the cache through `AuthCache` |
| `AuthCache` | class | the one service-facing facade over the existing adapter; absorbs `TokenStore` |
| `decideAccess(claims, ctx)` | pure function (policy module) | the former `RequestPolicy`; no state, no I/O |

- `RequestPolicy` is not a class: the plan describes it as stateless with no side effects (`PLAN.md:12-13`), so it ships as a pure exported function.
- `TokenStore` is folded into `AuthCache`: the plan gives it no responsibility distinct from the facade over the one backing cache (`PLAN.md:20-21, 45`). Upgrade trigger: if implementation finds a responsibility the adapter does not own (e.g. refresh-token persistence), split it back out as a plain module and record the reason.

### Wiring (D2, approved)
One composition root creates a single `AuthCache(adapter)` and passes it to
`new AuthBroker(cache, ...)` and `new SessionMint(cache, ...)`. No module-level
export of the instance. Tests construct their own `AuthCache` over a fake adapter.

### Concurrent-mutation guard (D3, approved)
`AuthCache` keeps a per-tenant invalidation generation. Every invalidation hook
(logout, revocation, suspension) bumps it. `put()` carries the generation
observed at read time and is dropped if the tenant's generation has advanced.
A dropped write degrades to a cache miss (one extra IDP call), never to a stale
allow. Facade-internal; the adapter is unchanged. Prune a tenant's generation
entry when the tenant is deleted so the map stays O(active tenants).

### Single miss path (D5, approved)
`AuthCache.getOrLoad(key, loader)`: read; on miss call `loader`; write through
the generation guard. Both `AuthBroker` and `SessionMint` use it; the key rule
(tenant ID + issuer + audience + policy version) is built in exactly one place.

### Request flow
```
 request(token, tenantCtx)
        │
        ▼
 AuthBroker.validateAndDispatch()
        │
        ├─► AuthCache.getOrLoad(key(tenant,issuer,aud,policyVer), loader)
        │        │ hit ──────────────────────────────► claims
        │        │ miss ─► loader: IDP validation calls ─► claims
        │        │                 (5 calls; sequential until the D8 commit,
        │        │                  then Promise.all fail-fast)
        │        └─ put(claims, genSeen) ─ dropped if tenant gen advanced (D3)
        │
        ├─► decideAccess(claims, tenantCtx)   pure; allow | deny
        │
        ├─ allow ─► dispatch(request)
        └─ deny  ─► explicit deny outcome
   any throw ─► single catch: error map (D4)
                 ValidationError  → deny 401 + log{tenant,reqId}
                 PolicyDenied     → deny 403 + log
                 IdpUnavailable   → 503 retryable + log
                 unknown          → deny + re-throw + log

 SessionMint.mint()/refresh() ─► AuthCache.getOrLoad(...) (same path, same guard)

 invalidation hooks (logout | revoke | suspend tenant)
        └─► adapter.invalidate(...)  +  AuthCache.bumpGeneration(tenant)
```

## Code quality (D4, approved)
`validateAndDispatch()` becomes a linear validate → decideAccess → dispatch
inside one `try`; a single `catch` maps each known error class to an explicit
outcome and a structured log line carrying tenant ID and request ID. Unknown
errors deny and re-throw. Deny-by-default is the contract: nothing reaches
dispatch after a failed validation. Table-driven unit test, one row per error
class. Existing ASCII diagrams in touched files (unknown until source is open)
must be checked and updated in the same commit.

## Tests (D6 and D7, approved)
**Regression contract (IRON RULE).** Before any rewrite, write a
characterization suite against `legacyAuthFlow()` covering: valid token,
expired, revoked, logged-out, suspended tenant, cross-tenant token,
policy-version bump, malformed token, IDP unavailable, IDP timeout. Assert the
outcome class and the resulting cache state. The new flow must pass the same
suite. Intentional differences are only D4's explicit deny where legacy
swallowed an error; each such case is listed and asserted as an intentional
change. Nothing else may differ. Shadow compare in production was not approved
(captured as TODO 1).

**Two-tenant E2E** against a fake IDP: tenants A and B log in, validate,
`decideAccess` and dispatch; a cross-tenant token is rejected; suspending A
mid-session denies A's next request and leaves B untouched; IDP outage yields
the explicit 503 path; a policy-version bump forces a re-validate.

**Common-work proof of retained contracts** (`PLAN.md:16-22`, no separate
approval): tenant-key isolation through the facade; logout, revocation and
suspension propagate through `AuthCache`, not just the adapter.

**Carried with approved remedies:** D3 deterministic concurrency test (write
started before invalidation is dropped); D4 table-driven error-map test; D5
`getOrLoad` hit / miss / loader-throws tests.

Test framework: unknown (repository holds no manifest or test files; CLAUDE.md
has no Testing section). Match whatever the auth package already uses; do not
introduce a new runner for this work.

## Performance (D8, approved)
The 5 IDP calls stay sequential through the refactor. `Promise.all` lands as
its own final commit on this branch after the characterization suite is green
against the new flow. Preconditions: a bounded probe confirms no call consumes
another call's output and the IDP tolerates 5 concurrent calls per validation;
fail-fast semantics with the first rejection routed through the D4 error map;
before/after validation latency recorded in the PR. The policy-version-bump
miss storm is existing behavior; single-flight de-dup is captured as TODO 2.

## Implementation order
1. Characterization suite against `legacyAuthFlow()` (must be green on legacy before step 8).
2. `decideAccess(claims, ctx)` pure function + table-driven tests.
3. `AuthCache` facade: key rule, generation guard, `getOrLoad`, invalidation-hook bumps, concurrency test, isolation/propagation tests.
4. `AuthBroker.validateAndDispatch()` rewrite with the error map + tests.
5. `SessionMint` on `getOrLoad` + tests.
6. Composition root: single `AuthCache` wiring; rewire callers of `legacyAuthFlow()`.
7. Two-tenant E2E with fake IDP.
8. Run the characterization suite against the new flow; list intentional D4 differences; delete `legacyAuthFlow()`.
9. Final commit: `Promise.all` after the independence and rate-limit probe; record latency.
